buildUp: Start with what catches the wind: three long, twisted blades on a hub, as large as can be built and transported, because energy grows with the area they sweep.
Put the rotor up high on a tall steel tower, built in sections that can travel by road, and anchor it on a massive concrete foundation so the wind can't push it over.
Carry the rotor's slow, heavy turning back into a housing on top of the tower: a main shaft held by a big bearing, all mounted on a stiff bedplate.

Speed the turning up with a gearbox, so a compact generator can turn it into electricity, then use a converter to match the grid's frequency and a transformer to raise the voltage for the trip down the tower.
Give the machine control over itself: pitch motors in the hub twist each blade to set the power and stop the rotor, and a high-speed brake holds it still for servicing.
Finally, let it follow the wind: sensors on the roof measure speed and direction, yaw drives turn the whole nacelle on its bearing, and a cooler on the roof uses the wind to carry away the heat.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Build a set of very long wings that slice through the air sideways, so the wind gives them lift rather than just pushing them, and put them as high and as large as possible because the energy grows with the area swept. Then let the machine constantly steer itself: turn to face the wind, twist its blades to take just the right bite, and gear the slow rotor up so a compact generator can turn its motion into electricity.

hardParts.title: Blades that are huge, light and tough
hardParts.why: A blade over 70 m long has to be stiff enough not to bend into the tower, light enough not to collapse under its own weight as it swings up and down every few seconds, and tough enough to survive hundreds of millions of load cycles, rain erosion at its tip and lightning strikes. Making something that large to aircraft-like precision, then moving it by road, is a feat in itself.

hardParts.title: A gearbox that survives an unsteady wind
hardParts.why: The gearbox carries an enormous torque that is never steady: gusts, turbulence and emergency stops send jolts through the gears thousands of times a day. Early large turbines suffered many gearbox and bearing failures, and replacing one at the top of a tower is expensive, so the gears, bearings, lubrication and the loads reaching them all need careful design.

hardParts.title: Making power the grid can use
hardParts.why: The wind's speed changes from second to second, and so does the generator's, yet the grid needs electricity at a precise frequency and voltage. The converter, generator and pitch control have to work together to smooth out gusts, keep power flowing during brief grid faults and shut the turbine down safely when it must.

principles.explanation: Because the power in the wind grows with the area swept and the cube of wind speed, turbines are built huge and put on tall towers where the wind is faster. In numbers, the power passing through a circle is half the air's density, times the area, times the wind speed cubed. Doubling the blade length quadruples the area, and doubling the wind speed gives eight times the power. Up on a tall tower the wind is also steadier than near the ground.
principles.title: Power grows with area and the cube of wind speed

principles.explanation: A wing-shaped blade moving sideways across the wind is pulled round by lift, so its tip can travel around seven to nine times faster than the wind. A windmill sail that the wind simply pushes can never move faster than the wind. Because the tip moves faster than the root, the blade is twisted along its length so every part meets the air at the right angle.
principles.title: Lift, not drag, turns the rotor

principles.explanation: A turbine can never capture more than 59.3 percent of the wind's energy, because taking it all would stop the air dead behind it and block the air coming in. The best possible compromise slows the wind to about a third of its speed behind the rotor; Albert Betz worked out this ceiling in 1919. Good modern rotors reach about 80 percent of that limit.
principles.title: You can't catch it all: the Betz limit

principles.explanation: Generators are smaller and cheaper when they spin fast, so a gearbox speeds the slow rotor up about a hundred times while dividing its turning force by the same amount. Power is turning force times speed. The rotor turns slowly with an enormous force, and the gearbox keeps the power almost the same, so a compact generator spinning at about 1,500 rpm can do the job.
principles.title: Gears trade turning force for speed

firstPrinciples.problem: Moving air carries energy, but it is thin, it never blows at the same speed for long, and it keeps changing direction. To turn it into useful amounts of electricity you have to catch the wind across a vast area, convert a slow, irregular push into the fast, steady spin a generator wants, deliver power that exactly matches the grid, and survive twenty-five years of storms, ice and lightning on top of a pole.

questions.answer: The energy captured grows with the area the blades sweep, which goes up with the square of the blade length, so longer blades catch much more. Higher up, the wind is also faster and less turbulent, and the power in the wind grows with the cube of its speed.
questions.question: Why are wind turbines built so tall, with such long blades?

questions.answer: Above about 25 m/s the forces on the blades, tower and gearbox would become dangerous. The turbine reaches its full power at about 12 m/s and holds it steady by pitching the blades, then feathers them edge-on and stops in a storm to protect itself.
questions.question: Why does a turbine stop in very strong winds instead of making the most power?

questions.answer: To capture all of it, the air would have to stop completely behind the rotor, and then no new air could flow through. The best balance, the Betz limit, takes at most 59.3 percent of the energy, and real turbines get to roughly half of the wind's energy at best.
questions.question: Why can't a wind turbine capture all the energy in the wind?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: A modern wind turbine works because it never stops adjusting. Its controller constantly reads the wind, turns the nacelle to face it, twists each blade a degree at a time and sets the generator's load, so the rotor always runs at the speed that captures the most energy and lets the excess slip past in a storm. Combined with sheer size, blades longer than a jumbo jet's wings on towers taller than most buildings, that turns a gentle breeze into enough electricity for thousands of homes.

name: Wind Turbine
overview:
A wind turbine turns moving air into electricity. Wind flowing over the long, twisted blades creates lift, just as it does on an aircraft wing, and that lift pulls the blades round. A big modern onshore turbine has blades over 70 m long sweeping a circle bigger than a football pitch, with its hub well over 100 m up, where the wind is stronger and steadier than near the ground.

The blades turn slowly, only about ten times a minute, but with enormous force. In a geared turbine like this one, the main shaft carries that turning force back into the nacelle, the housing on top of the tower, where a gearbox speeds it up roughly a hundred times so a compact generator can spin at around 1,500 revolutions a minute. A power converter then tidies the electricity to match the grid, and a transformer steps it up to a higher voltage to send down the tower.

The turbine constantly adjusts itself. Sensors on the roof measure the wind; yaw motors turn the whole nacelle on a giant bearing to face into it, and pitch motors in the hub twist each blade to take just the right bite of air, feathering them in storms. A turbine like this makes power in winds from about 3 m/s, a light breeze, and shuts down above about 25 m/s to protect itself.

parts.description: Long, hollow, gently twisted wing that turns the wind's push into a slow, powerful spin of the hub.

details.didYouKnow: Three blades won out over two or four because three gives a smooth, balanced rotor without the cost of a fourth blade. A two-blade rotor wobbles as it turns towards the tower, and it spins faster and noisier.
details.howItWorks: Each blade is a long wing. Air flowing over its curved shape is turned slightly, and the reaction pushes the blade sideways, which is lift, just as on an aircraft wing. Because the blade is spinning, its tip moves far faster than its root, so it is twisted along its length to meet the air at the best angle everywhere. Together, the three blades catch the wind across a circle that on the largest turbines is bigger than two football pitches.
keyNumbers: About 73 m long on a V150-class turbine
Roughly 20 to 25 tonnes each
Tips move at up to about 300 km/h
About 10 to 12 turns a minute
details.madeOf: Glass fibre and epoxy resin laid up in two huge half-moulds and glued together, around a stiff internal spar made with carbon fibre or glass fibre, with balsa wood or foam cores to keep the skins stiff. A copper lightning conductor runs down the inside to receptors in the tip.

parts.name: Blade

parts.description: Huge ring bearing at the root of each blade that lets the blade twist about its own length.

details.didYouKnow: Pitch bearings never spin round fully; they rock back and forth over small angles millions of times. That kind of motion is hard on grease and balls, so these bearings are one of the trickiest parts to design.
details.howItWorks: The pitch bearing joins the blade root to the hub while letting the blade turn about its own length. In light winds the blades are pitched to take the biggest bite of air; as the wind rises past the turbine's full power, they are turned to let more wind slip past, keeping the power steady. In a storm, or to stop the turbine, the blades are feathered edge-on to the wind, which works as the main brake.
keyNumbers: Roughly 3 to 4 m across
Turns the blade through about 90 degrees
Pitch speed of several degrees per second
details.madeOf: Two huge rings of forged steel with rows of steel balls between them, sealed and greased, with gear teeth cut into the inner ring for the pitch motor's pinion. Hundreds of bolts fix it to the hub on one side and the blade root on the other.

parts.name: Pitch bearing

parts.description: Electric motor and gearbox inside the hub that turns a blade on its bearing, a degree at a time.

details.didYouKnow: Some turbines adjust each blade separately as it goes round, because the wind is usually stronger at the top of the circle than at the bottom. Easing each blade a little at the top evens out the load and reduces fatigue.
details.howItWorks: The control system constantly works out the best angle for each blade and tells the pitch motors to set it. Each motor drives a small gearbox and pinion that turns the toothed ring of its pitch bearing. Every blade has its own motor, so if one fails the other two can still feather and stop the rotor safely, and batteries or ultracapacitors in the hub keep them working even if the grid power is lost.
keyNumbers: One per blade
Backup power to feather the blades on its own
Blade angle adjusted many times a minute
details.madeOf: An electric motor and a planetary gearbox in steel and cast-iron housings, controlled by drives in cabinets inside the hub. Some turbines use hydraulic cylinders for pitch instead, but the idea is the same.

parts.name: Pitch motor

parts.description: Cast-iron heart of the rotor that the three blades bolt to, carrying their whole load onto the main shaft.

details.didYouKnow: A hub like this is one of the largest iron castings in common use. Big castings are hard to get right, because the iron cools slowly in the middle, so foundries model the cooling by computer before they pour.
details.howItWorks: The hub is the heart of the rotor. The three blades bolt to it through their pitch bearings, and it carries their combined thrust, weight and turning force onto the main shaft. Inside it are the pitch motors, their control cabinets and backup batteries, and there is room for technicians to climb in from the nacelle to service them.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 to 5 m across
Several tens of tonnes as a casting
Carries the force of all three blades
details.madeOf: A single casting of ductile iron, a tough form of cast iron with tiny graphite spheres in it that let it bend slightly rather than crack. It is machined at its flanges so the bearings and shaft bolt on accurately.

parts.name: Hub

parts.description: Smooth glass-fibre cover over the front of the hub that keeps rain out and lets technicians work inside.

details.didYouKnow: The nose cone points into the wind on most modern turbines, which are upwind designs: the rotor sits in front of the tower so the blades never pass through the tower's wind shadow.
details.howItWorks: The nose cone, or spinner, covers the front of the hub. It does a little to smooth the air flowing past the blade roots, but mainly it is a weatherproof shell that keeps rain, snow and birds away from the pitch system and gives technicians a dry place to work inside the hub.
keyNumbers: Roughly 5 m across at the back
Only a few millimetres to a few centimetres thick
Bolted on in panels so it can be fitted at height
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic panels bolted to a light steel frame mounted on the hub, painted white or light grey like the blades and tower.

parts.name: Nose cone

parts.description: Thick forged steel shaft that carries the rotor's slow, enormous turning force back into the nacelle.

details.didYouKnow: The force twisting the main shaft of a big turbine is like several thousand people all hanging off the end of a 1 m spanner at once.
details.howItWorks: The rotor turns slowly but with a huge twisting force, and the main shaft carries it back from the hub into the gearbox. It also carries the rotor's weight and the bending loads from gusts, passing those down through the main bearing to the bedplate so that only the turning force reaches the gears.
keyNumbers: Turns at about 10 rpm
Carries a torque of several thousand kilonewton-metres
Tens of tonnes of forged steel
details.madeOf: A single forging of high-strength alloy steel, often hollow so cables and hydraulic lines can pass through to the hub. Forging lines up the grain of the steel along the shaft, which makes it resist fatigue far better than a casting.

parts.name: Main shaft

parts.description: Large roller bearing that holds up the shaft and the weight of the rotor while letting it turn.

details.didYouKnow: Changing a main bearing usually means lifting the whole rotor off with a huge crane, so engineers work hard to make this part last the turbine's whole life.
details.howItWorks: The main bearing holds the shaft up and keeps it steady while it turns. As well as the weight of the rotor, it has to take the push of the wind on the blades, which tries to shove the whole rotor backwards, and the bending loads as gusts hit one blade harder than another.
keyNumbers: Bore of roughly 1 m or more
Takes a rotor thrust of roughly 1,000 kN, about 100 tonnes of push
Designed to last about 20 to 25 years
details.madeOf: A large spherical or tapered roller bearing of hardened bearing steel, set in a cast-iron housing bolted to the bedplate. The rollers run in grease or oil, with seals to keep out moisture and dirt.

parts.name: Main bearing

parts.description: Planetary and parallel gear stages that speed the shaft up about a hundred times for the generator.

details.didYouKnow: Early large turbines gained a reputation for gearbox failures, which led some makers to build direct-drive turbines with no gearbox at all and a huge, slow generator instead. Both designs are common today.
details.howItWorks: A compact generator needs to spin fast, but the rotor turns only about ten times a minute. The gearbox steps that up roughly a hundred times. Planetary stages come first: a central sun gear, several planet gears and an outer ring share the huge torque between many teeth at once. A final parallel stage of ordinary gears raises the speed again and offsets the output shaft.
keyNumbers: Ratio of roughly 100 to 1
Input about 10 rpm, output about 1,500 rpm
Weighs several tens of tonnes
Loses only about 2 to 3 percent of the power
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel gears, ground to a very fine finish, running in oil inside a cast-iron housing. A pump circulates and filters the oil and passes it through the cooler on the roof.

parts.name: Gearbox

parts.description: Steel disc on the gearbox's fast output shaft, gripped by calipers to hold the rotor still for servicing.

details.didYouKnow: Before anyone climbs into the hub, the rotor is also locked with big steel pins that slide into holes in the main shaft or hub. The brake alone isn't trusted to keep people safe.
details.howItWorks: The main way to stop a turbine is to feather the blades so the wind no longer drives them. Once the rotor has slowed, hydraulic calipers clamp pads onto this steel disc to bring it to a stop and hold it there. Because the disc is on the fast side of the gearbox, a small brake can hold back a huge rotor.
keyNumbers: Disc roughly 1 to 1.5 m across
Acts on a shaft turning at about 1,500 rpm
Holds the rotor still for maintenance
details.madeOf: A steel disc on the gearbox's high-speed output shaft, gripped by hydraulic calipers with heat-resistant friction pads, much like a car's disc brake but larger.

parts.name: High-speed brake

parts.description: Short shaft with flexible joints that links gearbox to generator and soaks up small misalignments.

details.didYouKnow: Stray electric currents from the generator can jump through bearings and pit their surfaces with tiny sparks, so insulating the coupling helps the gearbox last longer.
details.howItWorks: The coupling connects the gearbox's fast output shaft to the generator. The two machines sit on separate mounts and flex slightly under load, so the coupling has flexible discs at each end that let the shafts be a little out of line without straining the bearings. It also includes a slip clutch that protects the gearbox if the generator jams or a fault causes a sudden jolt.
keyNumbers: Turns at about 1,500 rpm
Allows a few millimetres of misalignment
Slips if the torque spikes too high
details.madeOf: A steel or composite tube with flexible steel or glass-fibre disc packs at each end, and electrically insulating parts to stop stray currents passing from the generator into the gearbox bearings.

parts.name: Flexible coupling

parts.description: Spins at about 1,500 rpm and turns the shaft's rotation into electricity using magnets and copper coils.

details.didYouKnow: One modern 5 MW turbine on a decent site makes roughly enough electricity in a year for several thousand homes.
details.howItWorks: Inside the generator a rotor carrying magnets or electromagnets spins inside a ring of copper coils. As the magnetic field sweeps past the coils, it pushes electrons round them and makes electricity, the same principle Michael Faraday discovered in 1831. Because the wind speed varies, the generator's speed varies too, so its output goes through the converter before it reaches the grid.
keyNumbers: About 4 to 6 MW from a V150-class turbine
Spins at roughly 1,000 to 1,800 rpm
About 97 percent efficient
details.madeOf: A stack of thin electrical-steel sheets carrying copper windings, round a rotor with either permanent magnets made with rare-earth metals or wound electromagnets. Water or air cooling carries away the heat from the windings.

parts.name: Generator

parts.description: Upper half of the glass-fibre housing that keeps the weather off the machinery inside.

details.didYouKnow: On some turbines you can land a helicopter, or at least winch people down, onto a platform on the nacelle roof, which is how many offshore turbines are reached.
details.howItWorks: The nacelle cover is a weatherproof shell round the machinery, keeping out rain, snow, salt and sunlight. The upper half has hatches in the roof so technicians can climb out to reach the wind sensors and the cooler, and roof panels can be opened so a crane can lift big parts in or out.
keyNumbers: Nacelle roughly 13 to 20 m long
About 4 m wide and 4 m tall
Whole nacelle weighs around 100 to 200 tonnes with everything inside
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic panels on a light steel frame, often with built-in lightning protection and walkways. Glass fibre is light, doesn't rust and can be moulded into big, smooth shapes.

parts.name: Nacelle cover (top)

parts.description: Lower half of the housing, with a floor hatch so parts can be winched up from the ground.

details.didYouKnow: Wind technicians work in teams and wear harnesses whenever they are near an open hatch or out on the roof, clipping on to anchor points built into the nacelle.
details.howItWorks: The lower half of the cover wraps round the floor of the nacelle. It has a hatch in the floor at the back, where the built-in service crane lowers a hook to the ground to winch up tools and smaller spare parts, without needing a big crane for every job.
keyNumbers: Service crane lifts roughly a tonne or more
Floor hatch opens over 100 m above the ground on a full-size turbine
Sealed against driving rain and snow
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic panels, bolted to the bedplate and the nacelle's internal frame, with a non-slip floor for technicians.

parts.name: Nacelle cover (bottom)

parts.description: Stiff steel and cast-iron frame that everything in the nacelle sits on, resting on the yaw bearing.

details.didYouKnow: The rotor tilts its shaft upwards by a few degrees on real turbines, so the bending blades don't hit the tower. This model leaves out that tilt to keep it simple.
details.howItWorks: The bedplate is the floor and backbone of the nacelle. The main bearing, gearbox and generator are all bolted to it, and it gathers every load from the rotor and passes it down through the yaw bearing into the tower. At the front it is usually a heavy casting; at the back, where the loads are lighter, it is often a welded steel frame.
keyNumbers: Front casting weighs tens of tonnes
Carries the whole weight of the nacelle and rotor
Bolted to the yaw bearing with hundreds of bolts
details.madeOf: A ductile iron casting at the front and welded structural steel at the rear, machined flat where the machinery and the yaw bearing bolt on.

parts.name: Bedplate

parts.description: Cabinet of power electronics that turns the generator's output into smooth electricity in step with the grid.

details.didYouKnow: Modern converters let a wind turbine help steady the grid, for example by riding through brief faults instead of tripping off, or by supplying reactive power to hold up the voltage.
details.howItWorks: The generator's electricity changes in frequency as the wind speed changes, but the grid needs a steady 50 or 60 cycles a second. The converter uses fast electronic switches to turn the generator's output into direct current and then back into alternating current exactly in step with the grid. It also lets the turbine control how much power it takes from the rotor, which helps it run at the best speed for the wind.
keyNumbers: Handles several megawatts
Switches thousands of times a second
About 97 to 98 percent efficient
details.madeOf: Cabinets of power semiconductors called IGBTs, mounted on water-cooled heat sinks, plus capacitors, filters, control boards and cooling pumps.

parts.name: Power converter

parts.description: Steps the voltage up so the power can travel down the tower with less loss.

details.didYouKnow: Many older turbines have their transformer in a small green box beside the tower base; newer, bigger turbines often put it up in the nacelle or at the bottom inside the tower.
details.howItWorks: The generator and converter work at under a thousand volts, which would need very thick cables to carry several megawatts down the tower. The transformer steps the voltage up to tens of thousands of volts, so the same power flows as a much smaller current, cutting the losses and the size of the cable. From the foot of the tower, buried cables carry it to the wind farm's substation.
keyNumbers: Steps up from below 1,000 V to roughly 33,000 V or more
Rated at several megavolt-amps
Over 98 percent efficient
details.madeOf: Copper or aluminium windings round a core of thin electrical-steel sheets, insulated with resin or special oils that resist burning. Keeping it in the nacelle saves a long, heavy low-voltage cable down the tower.

parts.name: Transformer

parts.description: Radiator on the roof where the wind itself carries away heat from the gearbox, generator and converter.

details.didYouKnow: Putting the cooler on the roof means the stronger the wind, and so the harder the turbine is working, the better the cooling gets.
details.howItWorks: Even at 97 percent efficiency, the gearbox, generator and converter turn a few percent of several megawatts into heat, enough to warm dozens of houses. Pumps circulate oil and water-glycol coolant through these parts and up to the radiators on the roof, where the wind blowing through their fins carries the heat away, often without needing fans at all.
keyNumbers: Gets rid of a few hundred kilowatts of heat
Works in air from about -20 °C to 40 °C
Uses the wind itself for free cooling
details.madeOf: Aluminium radiator cores with thin fins, in a steel frame mounted on top of the nacelle, connected to the machinery by insulated pipes.

parts.name: Cooler

parts.description: Small mast on the roof that holds the wind sensors clear of the nacelle's own disturbed air.

details.didYouKnow: Because the rotor disturbs the wind behind it, turbines are calibrated so the controller can work out the real free wind speed from what the roof sensors measure.
details.howItWorks: The air just above the nacelle is stirred up by the rotor and by the nacelle itself, so the mast holds the wind sensors up and out on a cross-arm to measure air that is as undisturbed as possible. Aircraft warning lights are usually mounted up here too.
keyNumbers: A couple of metres tall
Usually carries two sets of sensors for backup
Often heated to stop ice building up
details.madeOf: Galvanised or stainless steel tube, with cables running inside to the controller, and often a lightning rod at the top to protect the sensors.

parts.name: Sensor mast

parts.description: Measures wind speed, so the turbine knows when to start, how hard to work and when to shut down.

details.didYouKnow: The power in the wind rises with the cube of its speed: twice the wind speed carries eight times the power. That is why a small error in measured wind speed matters a lot.
details.howItWorks: The anemometer measures wind speed. The controller uses it to decide when there is enough wind to start, about 3 m/s, how to set the blades and generator, and when the wind is too strong, around 25 m/s, so the turbine must feather its blades and shut down.
keyNumbers: Cut-in at about 3 m/s
Full power from about 11 to 13 m/s
Shuts down at about 25 m/s
details.madeOf: Either a classic cup anemometer, three cups on arms spinning on a bearing, or an ultrasonic sensor with no moving parts that times sound pulses across a small gap, usually heated against ice.

parts.name: Anemometer

parts.description: Measures wind direction, telling the yaw drives which way to turn the nacelle.

details.didYouKnow: A rotor that faces 10 degrees off the wind loses roughly 3 percent of its power, so good yaw control quietly adds up to a lot of electricity over a year.
details.howItWorks: The wind vane measures which way the wind is blowing relative to the nacelle. If the wind stays a few degrees off to one side for long enough, the controller starts the yaw drives and turns the nacelle until the rotor faces squarely into it again. It waits a little first, so it doesn't chase every brief gust.
keyNumbers: Accurate to a few degrees
Yaw usually starts after a sustained error of several degrees
Facing a few degrees off the wind costs measurable power
details.madeOf: A small plastic or metal fin on a low-friction bearing with an angle sensor, or the same ultrasonic sensor that measures wind speed, which can sense direction too.

parts.name: Wind vane

parts.description: Small hoist on a rail under the roof that lifts tools and spare parts up through the floor hatch and along the nacelle.

details.didYouKnow: Some newer turbines have built-in cranes strong enough to swap major parts without hiring a giant crane, which can save a great deal on a remote site.
details.howItWorks: Technicians cannot carry heavy tools and spares up a tower ladder, so a small electric hoist on a rail under the roof lifts them up through a hatch in the nacelle floor. The trolley then runs along the rail to wherever the work is. It handles filters, pumps and toolboxes, while the largest parts, like a gearbox, still need a big crane brought to the site.
keyNumbers: Typically lifts around a tonne or more
Reaches a floor hatch at the back of the nacelle
Lift height is the whole tower
details.madeOf: A steel rail bolted to the nacelle frame, a travelling trolley and an electric chain hoist with a load-rated hook. It is tested and certified regularly, like any lifting gear.

parts.name: Service crane

parts.description: Giant toothed ring bearing between tower and nacelle that lets the whole top of the turbine turn.

details.didYouKnow: The cables running down the tower twist as the nacelle turns, so the controller counts the turns and, after two or three in the same direction, unwinds them by turning back the other way.
details.howItWorks: The yaw bearing sits on top of the tower and carries the whole nacelle and rotor, while letting them turn to face the wind. It has to take the weight, the thrust of the wind trying to tip the turbine over and the twisting from uneven gusts. A ring of gear teeth cut into it gives the yaw drives something to push against.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 to 5 m across
Carries a few hundred tonnes of nacelle and rotor
Lets the nacelle turn a full circle several times
details.madeOf: Two huge forged steel rings with balls or rollers between them, or on some turbines plain sliding pads, with gear teeth cut into one ring and brake calipers gripping a steel brake disc.

parts.name: Yaw bearing

parts.description: Geared motor on the bedplate whose small pinion walks round the yaw ring to turn the nacelle into the wind.

details.didYouKnow: Turning a nacelle that weighs as much as a few hundred cars takes surprisingly gentle motors, because the yaw gears trade speed for force: a full turn can take ten minutes or more.
details.howItWorks: Each yaw drive is an electric motor driving a gearbox with a very high ratio, ending in a small toothed pinion that meshes with the teeth on the yaw bearing's ring. When the wind vane reports that the wind has swung round, all the drives turn together and their pinions walk round the ring, slowly turning the whole nacelle and rotor to face the wind again. When they stop, brakes in the motors and on the ring hold the nacelle still.
keyNumbers: Typically 6 to 10 drives on a large turbine
Nacelle turns at roughly half a degree per second
Gear ratios of about 1,000 to 1
details.madeOf: An electric motor with a built-in brake, on top of a multi-stage planetary gearbox in a cast-iron housing, with a hardened steel pinion at the bottom. The gearbox multiplies the motor's small turning force many hundreds of times.

parts.name: Yaw drive 1

parts.description: Geared motor on the bedplate whose small pinion walks round the yaw ring to turn the nacelle into the wind.

details.didYouKnow: Turning a nacelle that weighs as much as a few hundred cars takes surprisingly gentle motors, because the yaw gears trade speed for force: a full turn can take ten minutes or more.
details.howItWorks: Each yaw drive is an electric motor driving a gearbox with a very high ratio, ending in a small toothed pinion that meshes with the teeth on the yaw bearing's ring. When the wind vane reports that the wind has swung round, all the drives turn together and their pinions walk round the ring, slowly turning the whole nacelle and rotor to face the wind again. When they stop, brakes in the motors and on the ring hold the nacelle still.
keyNumbers: Typically 6 to 10 drives on a large turbine
Nacelle turns at roughly half a degree per second
Gear ratios of about 1,000 to 1
details.madeOf: An electric motor with a built-in brake, on top of a multi-stage planetary gearbox in a cast-iron housing, with a hardened steel pinion at the bottom. The gearbox multiplies the motor's small turning force many hundreds of times.

parts.name: Yaw drive 2

parts.description: Geared motor on the bedplate whose small pinion walks round the yaw ring to turn the nacelle into the wind.

When they stop, brakes in the motors and on the ring hold the nacelle still.

Nacelle turns at roughly half a degree per second
Gear ratios of about 1,000 to 1
details.madeOf: An electric motor with a built-in brake, on top of a multi-stage planetary gearbox in a cast-iron housing, with a hardened steel pinion at the bottom. The gearbox multiplies the motor's small turning force many hundreds of times.

parts.name: Yaw drive 3

parts.description: Geared motor on the bedplate whose small pinion walks round the yaw ring to turn the nacelle into the wind.

details.didYouKnow: Turning a nacelle that weighs as much as a few hundred cars takes surprisingly gentle motors, because the yaw gears trade speed for force: a full turn can take ten minutes or more.
details.howItWorks: Each yaw drive is an electric motor driving a gearbox with a very high ratio, ending in a small toothed pinion that meshes with the teeth on the yaw bearing's ring. When the wind vane reports that the wind has swung round, all the drives turn together and their pinions walk round the ring, slowly turning the whole nacelle and rotor to face the wind again. When they stop, brakes in the motors and on the ring hold the nacelle still.
keyNumbers: Typically 6 to 10 drives on a large turbine
Nacelle turns at roughly half a degree per second
Gear ratios of about 1,000 to 1
details.madeOf: An electric motor with a built-in brake, on top of a multi-stage planetary gearbox in a cast-iron housing, with a hardened steel pinion at the bottom. The gearbox multiplies the motor's small turning force many hundreds of times.

parts.name: Yaw drive 4

parts.description: Widest and thickest of the three rolled-steel tubes, bolted to the foundation.

details.didYouKnow: Tall towers are limited by roads: a tube much wider than about 4.5 m can't fit under bridges. Very tall towers are therefore built from concrete rings at the bottom, or from bolted steel panels.
details.howItWorks: The tower lifts the rotor high into stronger, smoother wind, and the bottom section takes the biggest load of all: the wind pushing on the rotor at the top acts like a huge lever on the base. That is why it is the widest and thickest part. Inside are the switchgear and controls at the foot, a ladder, and a small lift running up the full height.
keyNumbers: About 4.5 m across at the base, close to the limit for moving by road
A whole tower is roughly 100 to 160 m tall on a V150-class turbine
Bottom section can weigh over 100 tonnes
details.madeOf: Steel plates rolled into slightly conical rings, welded together into a tube with heavy bolting flanges at each end, painted to resist corrosion. The base plates can be over 5 cm thick.

parts.name: Bottom tower section

parts.description: Second steel tube, flanged and bolted to the sections above and below it.

details.didYouKnow: Towers are made in sections because one long tube couldn't be transported. Each section is lifted by crane and bolted to the one below from inside, by technicians standing on the platform at the joint.
details.howItWorks: The middle section carries the load down from the top while tapering gently, using just enough steel for the forces at its height. The tower is designed not only to be strong but to have the right natural frequency, so the passing blades don't set it swaying in resonance.
keyNumbers: Usually 20 to 30 m long per section on full-size turbines
Hundreds of bolts at each flange
The top can sway up to about a metre in strong winds
details.madeOf: Rolled and welded steel plate, thinner than at the base, with bolted flanges at each end and platforms inside at each joint.

parts.name: Middle tower section

parts.description: Narrowest steel tube, carrying the yaw bearing and the whole nacelle on its top flange.

details.didYouKnow: The crane that lifts a big nacelle into place can be well over 150 m tall itself, and a whole turbine can be put up in a few days once the foundation is ready.
details.howItWorks: The top section is the narrowest and lightest, and its top flange is machined flat so the yaw bearing can be bolted on accurately. The nacelle, hub and blades are lifted up separately by a giant crane and fixed on top.
keyNumbers: About 3 m across at the top
Carries a few hundred tonnes of nacelle and rotor
Top flange machined flat to within about a millimetre
details.madeOf: Rolled and welded steel plate with a heavy machined flange at the top, painted white or light grey to blend in with the sky.

parts.name: Top tower section

parts.description: Steel door at the foot of the tower where technicians go in to climb or ride the lift to the top.

details.didYouKnow: Because cutting a doorway weakens the tube, the steel round the door is reinforced with a thick frame so the tower stays just as strong there as everywhere else.
details.howItWorks: The door at the foot of the tower is how technicians get in. Inside are the turbine's switchgear and controls, then a ladder with a safety rail, or a small lift, running all the way up to the nacelle.
keyNumbers: About 1 m wide and 2 m tall
Lift ride to the top takes a few minutes
Climbing a 100 m tower by ladder can take 20 minutes or more
details.madeOf: A steel door in a reinforced frame cut into the bottom section, with seals against weather and a lock, usually reached by a short flight of steps.

parts.name: Tower door

parts.description: Heavy cables that hang free down the middle of the upper tower, so they can twist as the nacelle turns instead of having to slide.

details.didYouKnow: Turbines typically unwind on a calm day when little power is being lost, which is why you may sometimes see one slowly turning its head with its blades parked.
details.howItWorks: The generator's power has to get from a nacelle that turns to a tower that does not. The simple answer is thick, flexible cables that hang freely down the centre of the upper tower, held in a loose loop, and that twist as the nacelle yaws. The control system counts the turns and, after a few in one direction, turns the nacelle back the other way to unwind them.
keyNumbers: Allowed a few full turns each way
Unwinding takes a matter of minutes
Usually several parallel cables per phase
details.madeOf: Copper or aluminium conductors in very flexible rubber insulation, gathered on a saddle at the top and clamped in spacers so they stay evenly spread as they twist.

parts.name: Hanging power cables

parts.description: Wide slab of steel-reinforced concrete buried under the tower that stops the turbine toppling over.

details.didYouKnow: Once the turbine is built, most of the foundation is covered back over with soil, so all you see is the tower rising out of a small gravel pad.
details.howItWorks: The foundation stops the turbine toppling over. The wind pushing on the rotor creates a huge overturning force, and the foundation resists it with its own weight and its width, like the wide base of a desk lamp. Long anchor bolts cast into the concrete clamp the tower's bottom flange down.
keyNumbers: Roughly 20 to 25 m across
Around 3 m deep at the centre
Several hundred cubic metres of concrete
Can weigh over 1,000 tonnes
details.madeOf: Steel-reinforced concrete poured into a round or octagonal slab buried just below the ground, with a raised pedestal in the middle and a cage of anchor bolts. Soft ground can need piles driven deep underneath too.

parts.name: Foundation

summary: A modern three-blade wind turbine: blades longer than a jumbo jet's wings turn a hub, a gearbox speeds up the slow spin for a generator, and the whole nacelle turns on top of a steel tower to face the wind.
